name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,355

clue.text: Carers listen out for opponents of devolution (12)

indicators.note: Letters put out are put out of the order they arrived in, so the two words before are respelt from scratch.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, twelve letters

explanation.surface: Care workers keeping an ear open for the people who want power kept in London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listen out for' is one everyday phrase, and the shuffle signal is the middle word of it, covered by the two either side. Devolution in Britain means handing powers from Westminster to Edinburgh, Cardiff and Belfast.
explanation.definitionFit: Centralisers want decisions taken at the centre, so they are precisely the people arguing against powers being handed out to regional governments.

clue.text: Ignore leftovers of roast? (4,8)

definitions.note: The second definition names a dish rather than offering a synonym, and it is plural where the answer is singular: one cut of meat is what is left of the roast.

blocks.note: to pass somebody over deliberately, making a show of not acknowledging them
the joint that came out of Sunday's oven, eaten the next day straight from the fridge

explanation.surface: Wondering what on earth to do with the meat left over from Sunday's roast.
explanation.walkthrough: The joint of meat and the gesture share a phrase: you turn a shoulder on someone you are snubbing, and a shoulder of lamb goes cold overnight. The question mark marks the second reading as the playful one.
explanation.definitionFit: To cold-shoulder someone is to snub them pointedly; a cold shoulder is also, quite literally, the roast joint served up the next day.

clue.text: Unaffected, as is to be expected (7)

definitions.note: The second definition is a phrase where the answer is an adjective: it points at the use in 'that reaction is only natural', which is what anyone would have predicted.

blocks.note: free of pose or pretence, behaving as you really are
what anybody would have predicted, with nothing surprising in it

explanation.surface: Someone taking bad news in their stride, exactly as everyone predicted they would.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unaffected' invites you to read someone left unmoved by events; the sense wanted is the other one, free of affectation. Nothing is spelt out of anything here — the two halves simply meet at a comma.
explanation.definitionFit: An unaffected manner is a natural one, and something that follows as anybody would expect is natural in the other everyday sense.

clue.text: Cock has no hesitation sleeping here (5)

definitions.note: The definition names a place by pointing at it rather than naming it: 'here' stands in for the noun, the spot the bird settles on.

indicators.note: To have no something is to be without it, so the letters that stand for the next word come out of what is left.

blocks.note: a rooster is the farmyard cock, here left without its hesitation
er is the noise of hesitating in print, and it is the pair of letters taken away

explanation.surface: A cockerel settling down for the night without a second thought.
explanation.walkthrough: Er is how hesitation is spelt on the page, and it happens to be the tail of the farmyard bird's own name. 'Here' does the defining, pointing at the perch rather than naming it.
explanation.definitionFit: A roost is the branch or rail birds settle on for the night, which is exactly the 'here' the clue points at.

clue.text: Cicero’s speech almost all raised money (5)

indicators.note: Almost all of a word is all of it bar the end, so the last letter never arrives.
This is a down entry, so anything raised has been carried up the grid and its letters read from the bottom.

blocks.note: the word ALL docked to two letters, then read up the column
tin is old slang for cash, still standard crossword currency

explanation.surface: A speech by Cicero that almost entirely succeeded in raising money.
explanation.walkthrough: Cicero pleaded and orated in one language only, so naming him is a way of naming it. The surface's 'raised money' is a single idea and the clue splits it down the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Cicero argued his cases in the tongue of the Roman republic, so the definition names the language by its most famous speaker.

clue.text: Small regular congregation composed of several parts (9)

blocks.note: s = small, the size on a clothes label
a regular pulse or a regular surface is an even one
a fold is the flock a minister gathers, from the pen sheep are kept in

explanation.surface: A small but faithful congregation drawn from several different groups.
explanation.walkthrough: A fold is a sheep pen, which is how a minister's flock came by the word. 'Regular' is the even-versus-odd sense, not the reliable one the pews suggest.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sevenfold has seven parts or comes seven times over, and seven is the 'several' the definition is keeping vague.

clue.text: Insurgent doing the rounds? (13)

definitions.note: The second definition is a participle phrase where the first is a noun: it points at the adjective, the literal sense of turning round and round.

blocks.note: one who takes up arms to bring the government down
going round and round — one full turn, then another

explanation.surface: A rebel making the rounds, dropping in on everyone in turn.
explanation.walkthrough: A revolution is both the overthrow of a state and one complete turn of a wheel, and the clue buys the second sense with an idiom that normally means gossip circulating.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurgent fighting to topple a government is a revolutionary; and since a revolution is also one full turn, whatever goes round is revolutionary literally.

clue.text: Notice Northern Irish party welcoming south makes sense (4,2)

indicators.note: To welcome somebody is to take them inside, so the letter named next goes within the word before it.

blocks.note: an ad is the notice you place in a paper
the Democratic Unionist Party, the largest unionist party in Northern Ireland
s = south, as on a compass

explanation.surface: Northern Ireland's unionists warmly making the south welcome, and worth noticing too.
explanation.walkthrough: Unionists are the last people the surface would have welcoming the south, which is the joke it is running on. The definition is the arithmetic idiom — a column of figures that comes to the right total.
explanation.definitionFit: When a story adds up, its parts agree the way a column of figures does, which is the everyday way of saying it makes sense.

clue.text: Releases first bit of steam between umpire’s decisions? (4,3)

indicators.note: The first bit of a word is the letter it starts with, so that opening letter alone is taken.
What sits between two things has one on either side, so the letter just taken goes in the middle of the two calls named.

blocks.note: a serve that clips the net and drops in is called a let, and the point is played again
the opening letter of STEAM
the call that sends a cricketer back to the pavilion

explanation.surface: Steam escaping in the pause between one umpire's ruling and the next.
explanation.walkthrough: Two different sports supply the two calls — one from the tennis net, one from the crease. The question mark owns up to steam contributing a letter rather than a cloud.
explanation.definitionFit: To let out a breath, a prisoner or a yell is to release it, and the phrasal verb is the ordinary way of saying so.

clue.text: Two sixes by daughter making striking impression (5)

definitions.note: The definition is a descriptive phrase rather than a synonym, and the missing article is the setter's compression: a vivid memory is one that makes a striking impression.

blocks.note: six is VI in Roman numerals, and it is written out twice over
d = daughter, as on a family tree

explanation.surface: Two sixes struck with the family watching, leaving everyone impressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' is the cricket word doing double duty: the sixes in the surface are hit, the answer means memorable. Two sixes here come to four letters, not to twelve.
explanation.definitionFit: Something vivid stays bright and sharp in the mind afterwards, which is what making a striking impression describes.

clue.text: Walk stiffly, stumped by deep furrow (5)

blocks.note: st is how a stumping is entered on a cricket scorecard, the keeper breaking the wicket with the batsman out of his ground
a rut is the deep groove a wheel wears into a track

explanation.surface: A stiff-legged walker brought up short by a deep groove in the path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stumped' reads as baffled and is the cricket dismissal, two letters long on the card. The stiffness in the definition is bearing rather than injury — chest out, shoulders back.
explanation.definitionFit: To strut is to walk with a stiff, self-important gait, which is the stiffness the definition has in mind.

clue.text: Common sense about new place for puzzle (7)

indicators.note: Something set about a thing is wrapped round it, so the word before closes over the letters that follow.

blocks.note: nous is the British word for practical common sense, borrowed from the Greek for mind
n = new
pl is how Place is shortened on a street sign

explanation.surface: Down-to-earth advice about moving somewhere new, offered as a brain-teaser.
explanation.walkthrough: Nous is everyday British for common sense, and 'place' shortens the way it does in a postal address. The definition is a verb — to nonplus somebody is to leave them with nothing to say.
explanation.definitionFit: To nonplus someone is to leave them so bewildered they have no reply, which is what puzzling them amounts to.

clue.text: With objection finally dropped, now allowed small hooter (5)

indicators.note: What a word does finally it does at its end, so only the closing letter of the word before is meant.
Something dropped is let go of, so the letter just identified never makes it into the assembly.

blocks.note: the last letter of OBJECTION is the one being let go
the word NOW handing over its own three letters
to let somebody do something is to allow it

explanation.surface: An objection dropped at last, so the little horn may now be sounded.
explanation.walkthrough: A hooter is a car horn, or a nose in British slang; the bird that actually hoots is the one wanted, in its undersized young form. 'Now' hands over its own letters untouched before one of them goes.
explanation.definitionFit: An owlet is a young owl, and an owl is the bird everyone knows by its hoot, so 'small hooter' names it twice over.

clue.text: Twister ruined a party (7)

blocks.note: a coat ruined on a nail has been torn
the article handing over its own letter
a do is the British word for a party or a function — the office do, the works do

explanation.surface: A whirlwind that wrecked somebody's party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruined' looks exactly like the anagram signal the surface is offering and turns out to be a plain synonym. Three pieces in clue order, with no instruction anywhere telling you to move them.
explanation.definitionFit: Twister is the everyday American name for the same spinning storm, so the definition simply swaps one word for the other.

clue.text: Produce finest garment, cut short (4,3)

blocks.note: what a farmer takes off a field in a season
the top prize or the top student is the finest of them

explanation.surface: Making the very best piece of clothing, then trimming it down.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole back half of the clue, not the one word 'garment'. 'Produce' is the farmer's noun here — what comes out of the ground — and not the verb the surface wants.
explanation.definitionFit: A crop top is a T-shirt cut off above the waist, so the definition describes it exactly: a garment that has been cropped.

clue.text: Exclusive group one got into bed with before (7)

indicators.note: Getting into something is climbing inside it, so the letter named before goes within what has already been assembled.

blocks.note: a cot is a small bed
ere is the poet's word for before
one written as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: The in-crowd that somebody slept their way into.
explanation.walkthrough: Ere is the old poetic 'before', long gone from speech and permanent furniture in crosswords. The single letter lands near the end, across the seam between the two words making up the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A coterie is a small circle that keeps other people out, and keeping others out is what makes a group exclusive rather than merely select.

clue.text: Scolded after delicate material ripped (9)

indicators.note: What comes after something follows behind it, so the scolding word is placed second even though the clue says it first.

blocks.note: lace is the fine openwork fabric of a collar or a veil
to rate somebody, in the older sense, is to tell them off sharply

explanation.surface: A telling-off that followed some fine fabric being torn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rate' meaning berate has nearly gone from speech and is alive in crosswords. 'After' is doing real work here: it sends the scolding to the back of the answer, against the clue's own order.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacerated skin has been torn open, and ripped is the blunter word for the same damage.

clue.text: Desirable partner’s unforeseen snag (5)

blocks.note: the one everybody in the village hoped to marry
the condition buried in the small print of an offer

explanation.surface: The perfect spouse, with a drawback nobody saw coming.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive 's is the only join, so the clue reads as one phrase and is two definitions end to end. Both senses come from landing a fish: one worth having, one you had not bargained for.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone a catch says they are well worth landing as a partner, and a catch is also the hidden drawback in an offer that looked too good.

clue.text: Inaccurate section of route (3)

indicators.note: A section cut from something is a continuous piece of it, so consecutive letters are taken from inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: three letters sitting in a row inside that word, starting one in from its front

explanation.surface: A stretch of the road that has been mapped wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: A three-letter answer hiding inside one short word is easy to walk straight past. The definition wants the sense in 'your sums are out by a mile' — wrong, rather than absent.
explanation.definitionFit: If a calculation is out, it is wrong by some margin, which is the everyday British sense of inaccurate.

clue.text: Herb’s moment on the radio (5)

indicators.note: What comes over the radio is heard and never seen, so the word is taken by its sound and not by its spelling.

blocks.note: a moment is a time, and said aloud that word is what goes into the grid

explanation.surface: A bloke called Herb finally getting his moment on air.
explanation.walkthrough: The h in the answer is silent, so the two spellings are indistinguishable out loud. 'Herb' with a capital reads as the American first name, which is the whole of the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: Thyme is the small-leaved kitchen herb that goes into stuffing and stews, so the definition names it by family.

clue.text: Utterly undistinguished? On the contrary (13)

blocks.note: extra means exceptionally, as in extra strong or extra fine
nothing about it stands out from anything else

explanation.surface: Somebody flatly rejecting the suggestion that a thing is thoroughly dull.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as wordplay the two pieces say 'very ordinary'; read as a sentence the clue denies exactly that. The word's history sides with the clue — it is Latin for outside the ordinary run of things.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: what is the contrary of utterly undistinguished is remarkable, and remarkable is what the answer means.

clue.text: Independent elected member is a little devil (3)

blocks.note: i = independent, the label beside a candidate standing for no party
an MP is a Member of Parliament, the person a British constituency elects to the Commons

explanation.surface: A member of parliament who sits for no party at all, and is a menace.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves come off a British ballot paper. 'A little devil' is what an indulgent adult calls a naughty child, and the answer carries that fond sense as readily as the demonic one.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp is a small mischievous demon, and the phrase for a naughty child says the same thing half-fondly.

clue.text: Awful chore, covering front of motor in this? (6)

definitions.note: The definition is a pointer rather than a word: 'in this' says the front of a motor is finished in the answer, so the clue names the stuff by what it is used for.

indicators.note: Something awful is in a bad state, and letters in a bad state are no longer in the order they were handed over in.
What covers a thing lies over it, so the shuffled letters close round the single letter that follows.

blocks.note: the five letters of chore in a new order, parting after the fourth
the opening letter of MOTOR

explanation.surface: Coating the front end of a car in shiny plating, and what a miserable job it is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awful' does the shuffling while reading as the setter's verdict on the job. The question mark carries 'this': the clue never names the metal, it points at what a bumper is plated with.
explanation.definitionFit: Chrome is the mirror-bright plating on bumpers and grilles, so 'this' points at what the front of a motor is covered in.

clue.text: Recipient of funds originally persuaded everyone to accept vote in favour (5)

indicators.note: What a word does originally it does at its start, so each of the two words hands over only its opening letter.
To accept something is to take it in, so the letters just found open up to hold what comes next.

blocks.note: the opening letters of those two words, in the order printed
aye is the yes shouted in a division of the Commons

explanation.surface: Everyone talked round at the start, then asked to back the motion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Originally' reaches across two words at once, which is what makes that opening pair of letters hard to spot. Aye is the parliamentary yes, from the ayes and the noes of a Commons division.
explanation.definitionFit: A payee is whoever a cheque or a transfer is made out to — the one the money actually ends up with.
